title: Unscheduled Treatment Plans: A Follow-Up Guide
meta_description: How to follow up unscheduled treatment plans: build the list, sort by reason, use respectful message templates, set stop rules and track booked treatment.
h1: Unscheduled treatment plans: how to follow up respectfully
dek: Patients accept treatment and then don't book, for real reasons. A practical routine for practice managers: build the list, match messages to the reason, know when a person should call, and measure what matters.
key_takeaways: Treat unscheduled treatment plans as a weekly list to work, pulled from your practice software and cleaned first.
Sort patients by likely reason (cost, fear, timing, forgetting) and match the message to it.
Hand clinical questions, hardship and part-complete treatment to a person, often the treating clinician.
Set stop rules and honour opt-outs straight away.
Measure replied, booked, attended and completed, not messages sent.
body_html:
Every practice has them: patients who sat in the chair, heard the plan, said yes, and then never booked the next appointment. Or they finished stage one and quietly didn't come back for stage two. These unscheduled treatment plans rarely show up as a problem on any single day, which is exactly why they build up.

The short answer: treat unscheduled treatment plans as a list to be worked, not a memory to be jogged. Pull the list from your practice software every week, sort it by the likely reason the patient stalled, send a short, respectful message matched to that reason, and hand the patient to a person (often the treating clinician) when the conversation needs judgement. Then measure booked and completed treatment, not just messages sent.

This guide sets out a practical routine a practice manager can run this month, with a segmentation table, message wording you can adapt, stop rules, and the numbers worth tracking.

Why do patients accept a plan and then not book?

Accepted treatment not booked is usually not a sign the patient disagreed with the clinician. More often, something in their life got in the way between the chair and the front desk. Common reasons include:

  • Cost and cash flow. The quote was fine in principle, but the timing wasn't, or they wanted to check what their health fund would cover first.
  • Fear or anxiety. Saying yes in the surgery is easier than picking up the phone to book something that worries them.
  • Timing and availability. Work rosters, school pick-ups, travel and shift work make the next suitable slot hard to find.
  • Forgetting. They meant to call back after checking their calendar, and then didn't.
  • Health fund limits. Some patients wait for annual limits to reset before continuing.
  • Life events. Illness, a new baby, a move, a bereavement. Dental care slips down the list for good reasons.
  • Unanswered questions. They weren't sure about an option, the sequence, or how long it would take, and didn't want to seem difficult by asking.

Cost is a real and measurable barrier. In the ABS Patient Experiences 2024–25 release, 25.2% of people aged 15 and over delayed or did not use a dental professional when needed in the previous 12 months, and 16.1% reported that cost was a reason for delaying or not seeing a dental professional. Those figures describe the whole population, not your patients, but they are a useful reminder that follow-up should open doors rather than apply pressure.

How do I build an unscheduled treatment list from our practice software?

Most practice management systems can report on treatment that has been planned or accepted but has no future appointment attached. The report name and filters differ between systems, so check your software's help pages or ask your vendor's support team for the equivalent of "treatment planned, not appointed".

Whichever report you use, aim for a list with these columns:

  • Patient name and preferred contact method
  • Treating clinician
  • Date the plan was presented or accepted
  • Stage reached (not started, part complete, waiting on next stage)
  • Any note on the reason for delay, if the team recorded one
  • Marketing and contact preferences, including any opt-outs

Clean the list before you contact anyone

Remove patients who have since booked, been referred elsewhere, declined the treatment, asked not to be contacted, or have passed away. Check with clinicians whether any plan has been superseded. A five-minute clean-up prevents the most awkward messages a practice can send.

Tip: capture the reason at the desk

The best time to learn why a patient isn't booking is at checkout. A simple, consistent note such as "wants to check health fund" or "will call after roster comes out" makes every later follow-up more relevant. Agree a short list of reason codes with the team so notes are easy to sort.

Segment by reason, not just by date

A single generic reminder treats every patient the same. Sorting the list by likely reason lets you send a message that actually addresses what is holding the patient back. If the reason is unknown, use a neutral check-in and let the reply tell you.

Likely reasonWhat helpsFirst contactEscalate to
Cost or health fund timingOffer a conversation about options, staging or timing, as discussed with the clinicianShort SMS offering a callTreatment coordinator or practice manager
Fear or anxietyGentle tone, no deadline, invite questionsSMS or email, patient's choiceTreating clinician or a trusted team member
Timing or availabilitySpecific appointment windows, early or late optionsSMS with booking link or call-backFront desk
Forgot or unclearA friendly nudge and an easy way to bookSMSFront desk
Clinical questionsA clinician answers, not a templateMessage offering a callTreating clinician
Life event notedPause and check in laterHold; personal message when appropriatePractice manager decides

What follow-up cadence should we use?

There's no proven ideal schedule for treatment plan follow-up, and it should reflect your patients and the type of treatment. As a suggested starting point to test and adjust:

  1. Day 2 after the appointment: a short check-in. Did they have any questions? Would they like to book?
  2. Around 2 weeks: a reason-matched message (see templates below).
  3. Around 6 weeks: a personal phone call from the front desk or treatment coordinator.
  4. Quarterly after that: a light check-in, until the patient books, declines, or asks you to stop.

For part-complete treatment, where a patient finished one stage but hasn't returned, the clinician may want a person to call earlier. Let the treating clinician set the urgency for their own patients; the cadence is an admin tool, not a clinical judgement.

Reason-matched message templates

Keep messages short, identify the practice, avoid clinical detail in SMS, and always give an easy way to reply or opt out. Adapt the wording to your practice's voice.

Day 2 check-in (any reason)

SMS template

Hi [First name], it's [Practice]. Thanks for coming in this week. If you have any questions about the plan Dr [Name] talked through, just reply here and we'll help. You can book here when you're ready: [link]. Reply STOP to opt out.

Cost or health fund timing

SMS template

Hi [First name], it's [Practice]. We know timing and cost matter when planning treatment. If it would help to talk through options or timing with our team, reply CALL and we'll ring you at a time that suits. Reply STOP to opt out.

Only mention payment options, staging or fees that your practice actually offers and that the clinician has agreed are appropriate for that patient. If you're unsure, offer the conversation rather than the detail.

Fear or anxiety

Email template

Hi [First name], we wanted to check in after your recent visit to [Practice]. Many people have questions or worries before starting treatment, and that's completely normal. If you'd like to talk anything through, or ask about what the appointment involves, reply to this email or call us on [phone]. There's no rush. Kind regards, [Name], [Practice]. To stop these emails, [unsubscribe link].

Timing or availability

SMS template

Hi [First name], it's [Practice]. We have some early-morning and late-afternoon times coming up for your next appointment with Dr [Name]. Reply with a day that suits, or book here: [link]. Reply STOP to opt out.

Next stage not returned

SMS template

Hi [First name], it's [Practice]. Dr [Name] asked us to check in about the next stage of your treatment. Reply here or call [phone] and we'll find a time that works. Reply STOP to opt out.

When should a clinician or a person call instead?

Automation is good at the routine: reminders, check-ins, and getting a reply. It isn't the right tool when the conversation needs judgement or empathy. Move to a phone call from a person when:

  • The patient replies with a clinical question, symptoms, or concern about the treatment itself. That goes to the clinician.
  • The patient mentions financial hardship, illness, a bereavement or another life event.
  • The plan is part-complete and the clinician has flagged that the next stage matters.
  • The patient has had two or more messages without a reply and is still on the list at the six-week mark.
  • The patient seems upset, confused, or unhappy with their care.

Make the handover explicit: who calls, by when, and where the outcome is recorded. A reply that sits unanswered in a shared inbox is worse than no message at all.

Stop rules and opt-outs

Good follow-up knows when to stop. Agree these rules with your team and write them down:

  • Stop immediately when a patient opts out, says they've decided against the treatment, or says they're going elsewhere. Record it and thank them.
  • Pause when a life event is mentioned, and let a person decide when, or whether, to reach out again.
  • Close the plan after an agreed number of unanswered attempts, with a note for the clinician to raise it at the patient's next visit.
  • Never imply a deadline or consequence the clinician hasn't stated.
Compliance note (general information, not legal advice)

Messages that promote services may be treated as commercial messages. ACMA's guidance on the Spam Act 2003 says you need consent, must identify yourself as the sender with contact details, and must make it easy to unsubscribe. The OAIC's APP 7 direct marketing guidelines require a simple means for people to opt out of direct marketing. If a message promotes a regulated health service, check it against Ahpra's guidelines for advertising a regulated health service. Get advice on your own consent wording and processes.

What should we measure?

Messages sent is an activity count, not a result. Track a short funnel each month, using the same definitions every time:

MeasureDefinitionWhy it matters
ContactedPatients on the cleaned list who received at least one follow-upShows whether the routine is actually running
RepliedContacted patients who responded in any way, including "not now"Tests whether your wording opens a conversation
BookedPatients who booked the planned treatment or next stageThe first real outcome
AttendedBooked patients who turned upCatches bookings that later fail or no-show
CompletedPatients who finished the accepted planThe outcome that matters to patients and clinicians
Opted out or closedPatients who asked to stop or whose plan was closedA rising rate suggests tone or frequency needs work

Review by reason code as well as overall. If cost-related messages get replies but few bookings, the problem may be the conversation after the reply, not the message itself. Whatever tool you use, keep the definitions fixed so month-to-month comparisons mean something; our page on source and conversion tracking explains how DrKing reports this.

A weekly routine for practice managers

  1. Monday: run the unscheduled treatment report and clean it.
  2. Monday: tag new entries with a reason code and the next contact date.
  3. Tuesday to Thursday: send the scheduled messages; work the call list.
  4. Daily: clear replies within the same business day and route clinical questions to clinicians.
  5. Friday: update outcomes (booked, declined, paused, closed) and note anything to raise at the team meeting.
  6. Monthly: review the funnel and adjust wording or cadence.

Unscheduled treatment sits alongside two related lists: patients who are overdue for a recall, covered in our patient reactivation guide and 12-month reactivation calendar, and patients who missed an appointment, covered in turning a no-show into a return visit. Keeping them separate stops patients receiving three overlapping messages in one week.

faq.q: What is an unscheduled treatment plan?
faq.a: It is treatment a clinician has recommended and the patient has accepted, or started, but which has no future appointment booked. It can be a plan that never started or a multi-stage plan where the patient didn't return for the next stage. Most practice software can list these patients so the team can follow up.

faq.q: How long should a practice keep following up accepted treatment that isn't booked?
faq.a: There is no fixed rule. Many practices set a limited number of attempts over a few months, then close the plan with a note so the clinician can raise it at the patient's next visit. Stop straight away if the patient opts out, declines the treatment or tells you they are going elsewhere.

faq.q: Should treatment plan follow-up be automated?
faq.a: Routine check-ins and booking nudges suit automation, as long as replies are watched and answered promptly. Conversations involving clinical questions, financial hardship, anxiety or a life event are better handled by a person, and clinical questions should go to the treating clinician.

faq.q: Can we mention fees or payment options in follow-up messages?
faq.a: Keep SMS brief and offer a conversation rather than detail. Only mention options your practice genuinely offers and that the clinician agrees suit the patient. Messages promoting services should meet consent, sender identification and unsubscribe requirements, and should be checked against Ahpra's advertising guidance. Seek advice on your own wording.
